Karen McNamara Australia is a generous and compassionate nation. Our society has been built upon a commitment to help those less fortunate and to look after our mates. Throughout the years Australia has had a strong social safety net for those in need. It is crucial that we ensure the sustainability of this safety net and guarantee that it will be there for generations to come. Over the past 12 months the federal government has spent approximately $150 billion on social services and welfare. This spending provides Australians with pensions, aged care, benefits to families and individuals, and the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Of this, the age pension is our largest welfare payment, totalling an estimated $44 billion in 2015-16. This represents close to 35 per cent of the Commonwealth budget. In the coming decade the costs of delivering these services will increase as our population grows and ages. The _Intergenerational_ _r__eport_ stated that the number of Australians aged 65 and over is projected to more than double by 2055. Future projections anticipate that by 2055 there will be approximately 40,000 people aged 100 and over. Payments made through age and service pensions are projected to increase each year, and in real monetary terms spending per person is projected to increase from almost $2,000 in 2014-15 to around $3,200 in 2054-55. Currently, this spending accounts for 2.9 per cent of our gross domestic product; without changes to how we deliver the age pension this amount will increase to 3.6 per cent of GDP by 2054-55. This is an unsustainable path for Australia. It is essential that we address the sustainability of Australia's pension system to ensure that we are able to provide for senior Australians in future years. The age pension provides support for 2.4 million Australians and contributes to a broad retirement income system, which also includes superannuation and voluntary savings. The majority agreed with the bill's main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted in favour of reading the bill for a [second time](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that they can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The bill (as amended) makes changes to the assets test for all means tested income support payments, including allowances and pensions. Firstly, it increases the threshold above which your assests are tested (known as "free areas") for the purposes of support payments. In other words, people on allowances or full pensions can have more assets than they currently can before those assets are included in their means testing - but not that much more. See the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd129) for the asset test limits. People on allowances whose assets are above the free areas will no longer be eligible for that allowance while pensioners whose assets are above the free areas will have their pensions reduced at an increased rate. If someone is no longer eligible for a payment as a result of the changes, the bill makes them eligible for a concession card (either a Health Care Card or a Commonwealth Seniors Health Card). Read more in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd129).

Karen McNamara The scheme creates barriers and disincentives for injured workers to recover at work—for example, by emphasising the medical, rather than the vocational nature of rehabilitation services. Furthermore, the scheme allows injured workers to make claims for conditions that are unrelated to work, and to undertake treatments that are not evidence based. The truth be known, some injured workers are not getting back to work as quickly as they should be. There is strong community expectation that those who can work, even if only part-time, should do so to their capacity. These factors are contributing to the Comcare scheme being looked upon in a negative manner by the broader community. The Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Improving the Comcare Scheme) Bill 2015 is part of a package of reforms that will rehabilitate injured workers and return them to work sooner. The government is also ensuring the long-term viability of the Comcare scheme. Importantly, the proposed measures will ensure that the Comcare scheme continues to provide eligible injured workers with income payments until pension age, and lifetime medical and rehabilitation expenses. The proposed changes will mean that injured workers will be better off in term of access to early rehabilitation, access to provisional medical expense payments, and that they are able to return to work and receive quality medical treatment and attentive care. In addition, claims and disputes will be processed more efficiently and quickly, and some claimants will be eligible to receive higher payments than currently received. The bill is an important step in modernising the Comcare scheme, which has not seen comprehensive reform since it was established in 1988. The bill implements in part recommendations of the review by Mr Peter Hanks QC, and Dr Allan Hawke AC, commissioned by the former government, in 2012. The speaker opposed the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Improving the Comcare Scheme) Bill 2015, arguing it would reduce worker compensation, restrict eligibility, and introduce punitive sanctions, with the ACTU estimating low- to medium-income workers could lose between $120,000 and $325,000 over 20 years.

The Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Improving the Comcare Scheme) Bill 2015 was supported to modernise the Comcare scheme, as return-to-work rates had fallen from 89% in 2008-09 to approximately 80% and a 2012 review found the scheme created barriers and disincentives for injured workers to return to work.

The Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Improving the Comcare Scheme) Bill 2015 reforms the Comcare scheme to emphasise vocational rehabilitation and earlier return to work, increasing the maximum lump-sum payment from $242,000 to $350,000 and introducing provisional medical payments of up to $5,000, while strengthening the distinction between work and non-work related injuries and implementing recommendations from the 2012 review by Peter Hanks QC and Dr Allan Hawke AC.

The Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Improving the Comcare Scheme) Bill 2015 was opposed because it would reduce compensation and protections for injured workers, including cuts to lump-sum and incapacity payments, new eligibility rules that exclude workers, and higher proof tests for designated injuries such as heart and blood conditions.

The speaker opposed the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Improving the Comcare Scheme) Bill 2015, arguing it cuts workers' compensation benefits and standards. Specific provisions criticised include making it harder to establish work-related spinal, cardiac and stroke injuries (Schedule 1), reducing incapacity payments for long-term injuries, and imposing more punitive sanctions than any other Australian workers' compensation scheme (Schedule 15).

The speaker argued the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Improving the Comcare Scheme) Bill 2015 reduces compensation for injured workers, particularly low- to middle-income frontline workers such as cleaners, construction workers, and security officer Rosa, through a step-down approach (90% income for first 13 weeks, 80% for next 19, then 70%), potentially forcing them back to work before medically safe and costing affected workers between $120,000 and $325,000 over 20 years according to the ACTU.

The Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Improving the Comcare Scheme) Bill 2015 increases employer responsibility for alternative work arrangements, requires injured employees to actively participate in rehabilitation, introduces provisional medical payments of up to $5,000, raises the maximum lump-sum payment from $242,000 to $350,000, and provides uncapped long-term care for catastrophically injured workers after three years.

I rise to remark upon the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 2] before the House. This is, by the way, the third occasion that this matter has been before the House. For those of us who find the government's agenda to be a bit of a chaotic blur, albeit a nasty one, this is a bill that will establish the Registered Organisations Commission. The commission will be headed by a registered organisations commissioner with greater investigative power than those available to the general manager of the Fair Work Commission. The bill also modifies disclosure requirements, increases red tape and regulates individuals who choose, often on a voluntary basis, to dedicate their time to an employer body or union in the same way that the chief executives of corporate boards are also having to do. You could be forgiven for being a little confused that we are back in this place debating this bill because this is the third time those opposite have brought this bill forward. The Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 2] was reintroduced to enhance accountability and transparency of registered organisations by aligning obligations, penalties and regulator powers with the Corporations Act 2001, including increased civil penalties, new criminal offences for serious breaches, and the establishment of an independent Registered Organisations Commission within the Fair Work Ombudsman.

The speaker argued against the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 2], stating it was a political attack on opponents rather than genuine reform, and noted that the previous Labor government had already strengthened transparency and penalties in 2012. He highlighted that employer bodies and unions both opposed the bill, and criticized Prime Minister Tony Abbott for using a royal commission to compel three Labor leaders (Kevin Rudd, Julia Gillard, Bill Shorten) to testify.

The government argued the bill would establish a Registered Organisations Commission to strengthen financial transparency, increase penalties, and introduce criminal offences for union misconduct, while denying claims of hostility toward unions and asserting the reforms would protect honest union members from corruption and scandal.

The speaker argued in support of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014, criticising union power and alleging corruption, and cited a 63% increase in shipping costs at Bell Bay Aluminium after coastal shipping reforms tied to unions.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 2], arguing it attacks unions and worsens inequality, and cited ACOSS data showing the top 20% of earners receive five times as much as the bottom 20% and economist Joseph Stiglitz’s view that unions are a key bulwark against inequality. Opposed the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, describing it as a cut to agricultural research and development spending and part of a broader pattern of cuts to research funding in Australia, and said her focus would be on the bill's impact on rural people, employment and productivity.

Register of Foreign Ownership of Agricultural Land Bill 2015

The Register of Foreign Ownership of Agricultural Land Bill 2015 establishes a register of foreign-owned agricultural land, administered by the Australian Taxation Office, requiring existing holdings to be registered by 31 December 2015 and new interests within 30 days. The register will collect data on property location, size, and interest size, with plans to expand using state and territory land titles data.
Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Fees Imposition Bill 2015

The Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Fees Imposition Bill 2015 introduces fees on foreign investment applications, shifting administration and enforcement costs from taxpayers to investors. For residential and agricultural properties valued at $1 million or less, the fee is $5,000, with higher fees for more expensive properties and commercial or business applications.

The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank Bill was moved for a second reading, with Australia becoming a founding member and contributing US$3.7 billion (US$738 million paid-in) to fund regional infrastructure, which the speaker argued will boost Australian trade and jobs.
Medical Research Future Fund (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2015
The Medical Research Future Fund (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2015 was moved for a second reading, with the amendments enabling the fund's effective operation at commencement.

Called on Labor to support its own former budget savings promises rather than only the government's, tabling the Labor 2013-14 Budget Savings (Measures No. 1) Bill to give effect to those measures.

Customs Tariff Amendment (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013

Moved that the bill be read a second time, proposing changes to remove carbon tax elements from customs duties on aviation fuel and reduce airline costs, including surcharges of between $1.93 and $7.25 per passenger.
